claim: When a clause after a temporal preposition such as before refers to future time, “we usually have a non-modal present tense (compare #I want to leave before it will get dark)”.
evidence_summary: Ch. 3, p. 191: “When adjuncts and the complements of temporal prepositions such as after, before, as soon as, etc., take the simple present, not the will construction, when the reference is to future time”, as in [34i] I’ll buy one when the price comes / ∗will come down, and “the grammar requires the unmodalised forms”. CGEL uses ∗ for ungrammatical and # for semantic or pragmatic anomaly (p. xii). On p. 702, Ch. 8 says of a #-marked example that it “certainly does not violate any rule of grammar”.
finding: The two chapters disagree on the hedge (“usually” against a requirement) and on the kind of deviance (# against ∗) for one construction. Ch. 3 states a rule of grammar; Ch. 8 a usual pattern whose violation is semantic or pragmatic. One of them needs to change.
inference: Is will after temporal before ungrammatical or anomalous?

evidence.passage: §6.3, p. 697. “we usually have a non-modal present tense (compare #I want to leave before it will get dark)”.
evidence.example: Ch. 3, p. 191 [34], with ∗will come down and ∗will stop raining.
evidence.establishes: The same constraint gets # and “usually” in Ch. 8 (p. 697), ∗ and “requires” in Ch. 3 (p. 191).
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.
